claim: Relief of ongoing pain is a potent motivator of behavior, directing actions to escape from or reduce potentially harmful stimuli.
source: Relief of ongoing pain is a potent motivator of behavior, directing actions to escape from or reduce potentially harmful stimuli.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that frames the study's motivation, drawing on established understanding of pain relief as a behavioral motivator.

claim: Relatively little is known about the modulation of pain relief and its corresponding neurochemical basis.
source: Whereas endogenous modulation of pain events is well characterized, relatively little is known about the modulation of pain relief and its corresponding neurochemical basis.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge, which is the motivation for the study.

claim: Relief perception was enhanced by active decisions in the wheel of fortune gambling task.
source: We found that relief perception was enhanced by active decisions and unpredictability, and greater in high novelty-seeking trait individuals, consistent with a model in which relief is tuned by its informational content.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract, supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Relief perception was enhanced by unpredictability in the wheel of fortune gambling task.
source: We found that relief perception was enhanced by active decisions and unpredictability, and greater in high novelty-seeking trait individuals, consistent with a model in which relief is tuned by its informational content.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract, supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Relief perception was greater in high novelty-seeking trait individuals.
source: We found that relief perception was enhanced by active decisions and unpredictability, and greater in high novelty-seeking trait individuals, consistent with a model in which relief is tuned by its informational content.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract, supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Relief is tuned by its informational content.
source: We found that relief perception was enhanced by active decisions and unpredictability, and greater in high novelty-seeking trait individuals, consistent with a model in which relief is tuned by its informational content.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, drawing an inference from the observed patterns of relief modulation.

claim: Levodopa enhanced information-specific aspects of relief modulation.
source: We found that levodopa enhanced each of these information-specific aspects of relief modulation but no significant effects of the opioidergic manipulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the pharmacological manipulation, supported by experimental data.

claim: Naltrexone showed no significant effects on relief modulation.
source: We found that levodopa enhanced each of these information-specific aspects of relief modulation but no significant effects of the opioidergic manipulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the pharmacological manipulation, supported by experimental data.

claim: Dopaminergic signaling has a key role in modulating the perception of pain relief to optimize motivation and behavior.
source: These results show that dopaminergic signaling has a key role in modulating the perception of pain relief to optimize motivation and behavior.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from the experimental findings with levodopa.

claim: Pain is modulated to help optimize the way in which it directs protective behavior.
source: Theories of pain have suggested that one reason pain itself is modulated is to help optimize the way in which it directs protective behavior (Walters and Williams, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: Pain is increased when learning and responding to it, but reduced in situations in which pain might actually interfere with optimal behavior.
source: For instance, if pain is increased when learning and responding to it, but reduced in situations in which pain might actually interfere with optimal behavior will have a greater long-term benefit (Fields, 2018; Seymour, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Whether the principle of pain modulation for behavioral optimization extends to relief has not been tested.
source: Whether this principle extends to relief has not been tested.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Endogenous modulation of pain involves opioidergic and dopaminergic neurochemical systems.
source: Endogenous modulation of pain involves a number of different processes mediated by distinct descending signaling pathways, and involves at least two critical neurochemical systems: opioidergic and dopaminergic (Bannister, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Opioid signaling plays a key role in behavioral relief motivation in rodents.
source: For instance, opioid signaling has been shown to play a key role in behavioral relief motivation (in rodents, Navratilova et al., 2015b), placebo analgesia (Benedetti, 1996; Eippert et al., 2009), conditioned pain modulation (King et al., 2013), and relief perception (Sirucek et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work in rodents.

claim: Opioid signaling plays a key role in placebo analgesia.
source: For instance, opioid signaling has been shown to play a key role in behavioral relief motivation (in rodents, Navratilova et al., 2015b), placebo analgesia (Benedetti, 1996; Eippert et al., 2009), conditioned pain modulation (King et al., 2013), and relief perception (Sirucek et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Opioid signaling plays a key role in conditioned pain modulation.
source: For instance, opioid signaling has been shown to play a key role in behavioral relief motivation (in rodents, Navratilova et al., 2015b), placebo analgesia (Benedetti, 1996; Eippert et al., 2009), conditioned pain modulation (King et al., 2013), and relief perception (Sirucek et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Opioid signaling plays a key role in relief perception.
source: For instance, opioid signaling has been shown to play a key role in behavioral relief motivation (in rodents, Navratilova et al., 2015b), placebo analgesia (Benedetti, 1996; Eippert et al., 2009), conditioned pain modulation (King et al., 2013), and relief perception (Sirucek et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Dopaminergic signaling plays a role in conditioned place preference induced by pain relief through activity in midbrain dopaminergic neurons.
source: Dopaminergic signaling has clearly been shown to play a role in conditioned place preference induced by pain relief (through activity in midbrain dopaminergic neurons, Navratilova et al., 2012; Navratilova et al., 2015a; Xie et al., 2014), suggesting similar mechanisms as in the well-studied role of dopamine in food rewards (dopaminergic 'wanting' versus opioidergic 'liking'; Barbano and Cador, 2006; Barbano and Cador, 2007; Berridge et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dopamine is involved in 'wanting' while opioids are involved in 'liking' of food rewards.
source: Dopaminergic signaling has clearly been shown to play a role in conditioned place preference induced by pain relief (through activity in midbrain dopaminergic neurons, Navratilova et al., 2012; Navratilova et al., 2015a; Xie et al., 2014), suggesting similar mechanisms as in the well-studied role of dopamine in food rewards (dopaminergic 'wanting' versus opioidergic 'liking'; Barbano and Cador, 2006; Barbano and Cador, 2007; Berridge et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work on reward processing.

claim: Dopaminergic signaling is implicated in inhibition of pain by extrinsic rewards.
source: Dopaminergic signaling is also implicated in inhibition of pain by extrinsic rewards, that is rewards external to the pain system (Becker et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: It isn't known which system (opioidergic or dopaminergic) primarily shapes perceived relief as a function of motivation.
source: Hence, whilst it is clear that both opioidergic and dopaminergic signaling play core roles in relief motivation, it isn't known which system primarily shapes perceived relief as a function of motivation.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Pain relief would be modulated by the value of information it carries.
source: We expected that pain relief would be modulated by the value of information it carries, as hence enhanced by (i) active vs passive reception and thus controllability, since this reflects potential to exploit relief information; (ii) unpredictability, since this reflects the extra information carried by surprising events, and (iii) trait novelty-seeking, since this reflects individual information sensitivity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: Increased dopamine availability would enhance phasic release of dopamine in response to rewards.
source: We expected increased dopamine availability to enhance phasic release of dopamine in response to rewards, and hence, to increase the effect of active compared to passive reception of pain relief.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors based on theoretical reasoning about dopamine function.

claim: Inhibition of endogenous opioid signaling would decrease the effect of active controllability on pain relief.
source: In contrast, we expected the inhibition of endogenous opioid signaling to decrease the effect of active controllability on pain relief. The latter is based on the observation that blocking of opioid receptors attenuates other types of endogenous pain inhibition such as placebo analgesia (Benedetti, 1996; Eippert et al., 2009) or conditioned pain modulation (King et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors, supported by citations to prior work on opioid receptor blockade effects.

claim: Blocking of opioid receptors attenuates placebo analgesia.
source: The latter is based on the observation that blocking of opioid receptors attenuates other types of endogenous pain inhibition such as placebo analgesia (Benedetti, 1996; Eippert et al., 2009) or conditioned pain modulation (King et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Blocking of opioid receptors attenuates conditioned pain modulation.
source: The latter is based on the observation that blocking of opioid receptors attenuates other types of endogenous pain inhibition such as placebo analgesia (Benedetti, 1996; Eippert et al., 2009) or conditioned pain modulation (King et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: N=28 healthy volunteers participated in the study.
source: To test these hypotheses, we employed a previously developed wheel of fortune task utilizing relief of a tonic capsaicin-sensitive thermal pain stimulus as 'wins', and allowing to quantify endogenous pain inhibition induced by gaining pain relief in active versus passive conditions (Becker et al., 2015). To test the roles of dopamine and opioids, we analyzed and report data of N=28 healthy volunteers who ingested either a single dose of the dopamine precursor levodopa (150 mg), the opioid antagonist naltrexone (50 mg), or placebo in separate testing sessions (double-blinded, placebo controlled cross-over, i.e. within-subjects, design).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the study sample.

claim: The study used a double-blinded, placebo controlled cross-over design.
source: To test the roles of dopamine and opioids, we analyzed and report data of N=28 healthy volunteers who ingested either a single dose of the dopamine precursor levodopa (150 mg), the opioid antagonist naltrexone (50 mg), or placebo in separate testing sessions (double-blinded, placebo controlled cross-over, i.e. within-subjects, design).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the study design.

claim: Participants received 150 mg of levodopa in one session.
source: To test the roles of dopamine and opioids, we analyzed and report data of N=28 healthy volunteers who ingested either a single dose of the dopamine precursor levodopa (150 mg), the opioid antagonist naltrexone (50 mg), or placebo in separate testing sessions (double-blinded, placebo controlled cross-over, i.e. within-subjects, design).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the drug dosage.

claim: Participants received 50 mg of naltrexone in one session.
source: To test the roles of dopamine and opioids, we analyzed and report data of N=28 healthy volunteers who ingested either a single dose of the dopamine precursor levodopa (150 mg), the opioid antagonist naltrexone (50 mg), or placebo in separate testing sessions (double-blinded, placebo controlled cross-over, i.e. within-subjects, design).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the drug dosage.

claim: A probabilistic reward schedule was implemented to allow assessment of reinforcement learning.
source: To allow also the assessment of reinforcement learning, a probabilistic reward schedule associated with the participants' choices in the wheel of fortune was implemented.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the task design.

claim: Participants rated the thermal stimulation as less intense after actively winning pain relief compared to the passive control condition in the placebo session.
source: Replicating previous results, in the placebo (i.e. non-drug) condition participants rated the thermal stimulation as less intense after actively winning pain relief compared to the passive control condition, as rated on visual analogue scales (VAS) from 'no sensation' (0) over 'just painful' (100) to 'most intense pain tolerable' (200).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the placebo condition, supported by experimental data.

claim: Participants rated the stimulation as more intense after actively losing compared to the passive control condition in the placebo session.
source: Furthermore, participants also rated the stimulation as more intense after actively losing compared to the passive control condition (Figure 2A; interaction 'outcome × trial type', F(1,1040)=64.14, p<0.001; pairwise comparisons: win: test vs. control p<0.001, standardized effect size d=0.16; lose: test vs. control, p<0.001, d=0.27).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the placebo condition, supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Perception of both relief and pain are enhanced by active (instrumental) controllability.
source: This shows that perception of both relief and pain are enhanced by active (instrumental) controllability, as hypothesized.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, confirming the hypothesis.

claim: Behaviorally assessed pain perception did not significantly differ between test and control trials after winning or losing in the placebo condition.
source: In contrast to the VAS ratings, behaviorally assessed pain perception did not significantly differ between test and control trials after winning as well as after losing in the placebo condition (Figure 2D; interaction 'outcome × trial type', F(1, 1040)=2.53, p=0.112).
evidence: This is a finding from the placebo condition, supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: After levodopa intake, one participant reported a weak feeling of nausea and headaches at the end of the experimental session.
source: After the intake of levodopa, one participant reported a weak feeling of nausea and headaches at the end of the experimental session.
evidence: This is a report of an adverse event observed in the study.

claim: In 32 out of 83 experimental sessions subjects reported tiredness at the end of the session.
source: In 32 out of 83 experimental sessions subjects reported tiredness at the end of the session.
evidence: This is a report of a symptom observed in the study.

claim: In 52% of sessions, participants reported that they did not know which drug they received.
source: In 43 out of 83 sessions that were included in the analysis (52%), participants reported that they did not know which drug they received.
evidence: This is a finding from the blinding assessment.

claim: In 43% of placebo sessions, participants correctly guessed they had received placebo.
source: In 12 out of 28 sessions (43%), participants were correct in assuming that they had ingested the placebo, in 6 out of 27 sessions (22%) levodopa, and in 2 out of 28 sessions (7%) naltrexone.
evidence: This is a finding from the blinding assessment.

claim: In 22% of levodopa sessions, participants correctly guessed they had received levodopa.
source: In 12 out of 28 sessions (43%), participants were correct in assuming that they had ingested the placebo, in 6 out of 27 sessions (22%) levodopa, and in 2 out of 28 sessions (7%) naltrexone.
evidence: This is a finding from the blinding assessment.

claim: In 7% of naltrexone sessions, participants correctly guessed they had received naltrexone.
source: In 12 out of 28 sessions (43%), participants were correct in assuming that they had ingested the placebo, in 6 out of 27 sessions (22%) levodopa, and in 2 out of 28 sessions (7%) naltrexone.
evidence: This is a finding from the blinding assessment.

claim: Participants rated the thermal stimulation as significantly less intense after active relief winning under levodopa compared to passive control.
source: As in the placebo condition, participants rated the thermal stimulation as significantly less intense after active relief winning in the wheel of fortune task, and as significantly more intense after receiving phasic pain increases ('losing') compared to the respective passive control condition under levodopa (pairwise comparisons: win: test vs. control p<0.001, d=0.31; lose: test vs. control, p<0.001, d=0.32; Figure 2B) as well as naltrexone (pairwise comparisons: win: test vs. control p<0.001, d=0.22; lose: test vs. control, p<0.001, d=0.27; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the levodopa condition, supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Participants rated the stimulation as significantly more intense after losing under levodopa compared to passive control.
source: As in the placebo condition, participants rated the thermal stimulation as significantly less intense after active relief winning in the wheel of fortune task, and as significantly more intense after receiving phasic pain increases ('losing') compared to the respective passive control condition under levodopa (pairwise comparisons: win: test vs. control p<0.001, d=0.31; lose: test vs. control, p<0.001, d=0.32; Figure 2B) as well as naltrexone (pairwise comparisons: win: test vs. control p<0.001, d=0.22; lose: test vs. control, p<0.001, d=0.27; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the levodopa condition, supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Participants rated the thermal stimulation as significantly less intense after active relief winning under naltrexone compared to passive control.
source: As in the placebo condition, participants rated the thermal stimulation as significantly less intense after active relief winning in the wheel of fortune task, and as significantly more intense after receiving phasic pain increases ('losing') compared to the respective passive control condition under levodopa (pairwise comparisons: win: test vs. control p<0.001, d=0.31; lose: test vs. control, p<0.001, d=0.32; Figure 2B) as well as naltrexone (pairwise comparisons: win: test vs. control p<0.001, d=0.22; lose: test vs. control, p<0.001, d=0.27; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the naltrexone condition, supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Participants rated the stimulation as significantly more intense after losing under naltrexone compared to passive control.
source: As in the placebo condition, participants rated the thermal stimulation as significantly less intense after active relief winning in the wheel of fortune task, and as significantly more intense after receiving phasic pain increases ('losing') compared to the respective passive control condition under levodopa (pairwise comparisons: win: test vs. control p<0.001, d=0.31; lose: test vs. control, p<0.001, d=0.32; Figure 2B) as well as naltrexone (pairwise comparisons: win: test vs. control p<0.001, d=0.22; lose: test vs. control, p<0.001, d=0.27; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the naltrexone condition, supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The effect of active relief on perception was significantly larger in the levodopa condition compared to the placebo condition.
source: Moreover, the effect of active relief or increases on pain modulation was differentially modulated by the drugs (Table 1; interaction 'drug × outcome', F(2, 1587.30)=4.52, p=0.011). Specifically, the effect of active relief on perception was significantly larger in the levodopa condition compared to the placebo condition (post-hoc comparison p=0.007, d=0.23; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding comparing drug effects, supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 3A and Table 1.

claim: No significant difference in pain modulation was found for naltrexone compared to placebo condition.
source: No significant difference was found for the naltrexone compared to the placebo condition (p=0.252, d=0.12).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparison of drug effects.

claim: Endogenous modulation did not significantly differ between the levodopa and the naltrexone condition.
source: Endogenous modulation did not significantly differ between the levodopa and the naltrexone condition (p=0.368, d=0.11).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparison of drug effects.

claim: Endogenous pain facilitation induced by actively receiving pain increases did not significantly differ between any drug conditions.
source: Endogenous pain facilitation induced by actively receiving pain increases assessed with VAS ratings did not significantly differ between any drug conditions (all post-hoc comparisons p's>0.591).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparison of drug effects.

claim: Participants showed significantly less behaviorally assessed sensitization in active compared to passive trials when obtaining pain relief under levodopa.
source: In contrast to the placebo condition, participants showed significantly less behaviorally assessed sensitization in active compared to passive trials when obtaining pain relief under levodopa (pairwise comparison test vs. control: p=0.020, d=0.11; Figure 2E) consistent with an extension of pain-inhibitory effects of winning pain relief through to the underlying tonic pain stimulus.
evidence: This is a finding from the levodopa condition, supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Under naltrexone, test and control trials did not significantly differ in the behaviorally assessed pain perception.
source: Under naltrexone, test and control trials did not significantly differ in the behaviorally assessed pain perception (Figure 2F) as for the placebo condition.
evidence: This is a finding from the naltrexone condition, supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Behaviorally assessed pain modulation did not significantly differ between placebo, levodopa, and naltrexone.
source: Across drugs, behaviorally assessed pain modulation did not significantly differ between placebo, levodopa, and naltrexone (interaction 'drug × outcome': F(2, 1592.73)=1. 87, p=0.154; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparison of drug effects, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Participants selected the color associated with higher likelihood for winning relief in 64% of trials in the placebo condition.
source: Participants selected the color of the wheel of fortune associated with a higher likelihood for winning relief in 64% (SD = 28%) of trials in the placebo condition, consistent with a reinforcement learning effect.
evidence: This is a finding from the placebo condition, supported by experimental data.

claim: Participants chose the color associated with higher likelihood for winning above chance on a group level in the placebo condition.
source: Thus, participants chose the color associated with the higher likelihood for winning above chance (χ2(1)=6.64, p=0.010) on a group level, indicating successful learning.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of choice behavior in the placebo condition.

claim: Under levodopa, participants' choices did not significantly differ from chance.
source: In contrast to the placebo condition (post-hoc comparison p<0.001), under levodopa and under naltrexone participants' choices did not significantly differ from chance (post-hoc comparisons p's>0.759).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of choice behavior in the levodopa condition.

claim: Under naltrexone, participants' choices did not significantly differ from chance.
source: In contrast to the placebo condition (post-hoc comparison p<0.001), under levodopa and under naltrexone participants' choices did not significantly differ from chance (post-hoc comparisons p's>0.759).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of choice behavior in the naltrexone condition.

claim: Choice behavior significantly differed in the placebo compared to the levodopa condition.
source: Correspondingly, post-hoc comparisons show that choice behavior significantly differed in the placebo compared to the levodopa condition (p=0.015) and compared to the naltrexone condition (post-hoc comparison p=0.004), while choices did not significantly differ between levodopa and naltrexone (post-hoc comparison p=0.915; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparison of choice behavior, shown in Figure 4.

claim: Choice behavior significantly differed in the placebo compared to the naltrexone condition.
source: Correspondingly, post-hoc comparisons show that choice behavior significantly differed in the placebo compared to the levodopa condition (p=0.015) and compared to the naltrexone condition (post-hoc comparison p=0.004), while choices did not significantly differ between levodopa and naltrexone (post-hoc comparison p=0.915; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparison of choice behavior, shown in Figure 4.

claim: Choices did not significantly differ between levodopa and naltrexone.
source: Correspondingly, post-hoc comparisons show that choice behavior significantly differed in the placebo compared to the levodopa condition (p=0.015) and compared to the naltrexone condition (post-hoc comparison p=0.004), while choices did not significantly differ between levodopa and naltrexone (post-hoc comparison p=0.915; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparison of choice behavior, shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both dopamine and opioids may have an influence on relief-related learning and choice.
source: This shows that both, dopamine and opioids, may have an influence on relief-related learning and choice.
evidence: This is an inference from the choice behavior findings.

claim: The proportion of participants who correctly reported the color associated with higher chance of winning was not above chance in any drug condition.
source: The proportion of participants who reported this color correctly was not above chance (binomial test: p's>0.5; placebo: 50%, levodopa: 37%, naltrexone: 39.3%).
evidence: This is a finding from the exit interview data.

claim: Participants' belief about which color was associated with higher chance of winning significantly influenced their choices.
source: Nevertheless, participants' belief whether one color of the wheel of fortune task was associated with a higher chance of winning or not significantly influenced their choices (p<0.001) and this influence on choices, and thus on learning, depended on the drug condition (interaction 'drug × belief': F(2) = 6.91, p=0.032).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the relationship between belief and choice.

claim: Successful decision-making was associated with contingency awareness in the task.
source: This suggests that successful decision-making was associated with contingency awareness in our task.
evidence: This is an inference from the relationship between belief and choice.

claim: The current data does not allow a conclusion on whether contingency awareness was a prerequisite for or a consequence of successful learning.
source: However, the current data does not allow a conclusion on whether this contingency awareness was a prerequisite for or a consequence of successful learning here.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in interpreting the data.

claim: Model 4 had the best predictive accuracy among the reinforcement learning models tested.
source: The best predictive accuracy was found for model 4 that used an individually scaled outcome sensitivity, and a sigmoid function to map expected values for the two choices to the drift rate of the diffusion process (Table 2; see Materials nd methods, section Estimation of prediction errors and their role in endogenous pain modulation for details on parametrization of reward learning models).
evidence: This is a finding from model comparison, shown in Table 2.

claim: Posterior predictive simulations from the best-fitting model appropriately describe the observed choices.
source: Posterior predictive simulations from the best-fitting model appropriately describe the observed choices (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from model validation, shown in Figure 5.

claim: None of the model parameters could exclusively explain the differences between levodopa and naltrexone compared to placebo.
source: However, none of the model parameters could exclusively explain the differences between levodopa and naltrexone compared to placebo: the 95% highest density intervals (HDI) for the difference between all group level parameters of the drug effect enclosed zero (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from model parameter analysis, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Prediction errors showed a significant main effect for the prediction of endogenous pain modulation indicated by VAS ratings.
source: Prediction errors estimated by using subject level parameters of the model showed a significant main effect for the prediction of endogenous pain modulation indicated by VAS ratings (F(1, 1600.3)=452.9, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of prediction errors.

claim: Outcomes that are worse than expected (negative prediction errors) were associated with increased pain facilitation.
source: Conversely outcomes that are worse than expected (negative prediction errors, occurring with pain increases) were associated with increased pain facilitation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical finding on prediction errors, shown in Figure 6.

claim: The more unexpected the relief, the greater the perception of that relief.
source: In other words, the more unexpected the relief, the greater the perception of that relief; and the more unexpected the pain increase, the greater the perception of that pain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the prediction error findings.

claim: The more unexpected the pain increase, the greater the perception of that pain.
source: In other words, the more unexpected the relief, the greater the perception of that relief; and the more unexpected the pain increase, the greater the perception of that pain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the prediction error findings.

claim: The effect of prediction errors on pain modulation showed a significant interaction with the drug condition.
source: The effect of prediction errors on pain modulation showed a significant interaction with the drug condition (F(2, 1599.5)=7.529, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of prediction errors across drug conditions.

claim: The negative linear relationship between prediction errors and pain modulation was significantly stronger for levodopa compared to placebo.
source: Post-hoc analysis confirmed that the negative linear relationship significantly differed from zero for all conditions (p's<0.001), but this relationship was significantly stronger for levodopa compared to placebo (p<0.001) with no significant differences for naltrexone compared to placebo (p=0.083).
evidence: This is a finding from post-hoc statistical analysis of prediction errors.

claim: There were no significant differences in the relationship between prediction errors and pain modulation for naltrexone compared to placebo.
source: Post-hoc analysis confirmed that the negative linear relationship significantly differed from zero for all conditions (p's<0.001), but this relationship was significantly stronger for levodopa compared to placebo (p<0.001) with no significant differences for naltrexone compared to placebo (p=0.083).
evidence: This is a finding from post-hoc statistical analysis of prediction errors.

claim: Relief is enhanced by unpredictability, and this effect is sensitive to dopamine.
source: Overall, this shows that relief is enhanced to unpredictability, and this effect is sensitive to dopamine.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the prediction error findings.

claim: No significant interaction of prediction error with drug conditions was found for behaviorally assessed pain perception.
source: No significant interaction with of prediction error with drug conditions was found for behaviorally assessed pain perception (interaction 'PE × drug': F(2, 1600.1)=0.96, p=0.384).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of prediction errors on behavioral measure.

claim: Greater individual novelty seeking is associated with greater relief perception induced by winning pain relief.
source: Previous data suggest that endogenous pain inhibition induced by actively winning pain relief is associated with a novelty seeking personality trait: greater individual novelty seeking is associated with greater relief perception (pain inhibition) induced by winning pain relief (Becker et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Endogenous pain modulation induced by winning was associated with participants' novelty seeking scores in the placebo condition, although this correlation failed to reach statistical significance after correction for multiple comparisons.
source: Similar to these results, we found here that endogenous pain modulation, assessed using self-reported pain intensity, induced by winning was associated with participants' scores on novelty seeking in the NISS questionnaire (Need Inventory of Sensation Seeking; Roth and Hammelstein, 2012; subscale 'need for stimulation' (NS)), although this correlation failed to reach statistical significance after correction for multiple comparisons using Bonferroni-Holm method (r=–0.412, p=0.073).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis in the placebo condition.

claim: A similar association between novelty seeking and endogenous pain modulation was found in the levodopa condition.
source: A similar association between novelty seeking and endogenous pain modulation was found in the levodopa condition (r=–0.551, p=0.013).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis in the levodopa condition.

claim: The higher a participant's novelty seeking score, the greater the levodopa-related endogenous pain modulation when winning compared to placebo.
source: More importantly, the higher a participants' novelty seeking score in the NISS questionnaire, the greater the levodopa-related endogenous pain modulation when winning compared to placebo (NISS NS: r=–0.483, p=0.034, Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis comparing levodopa to placebo, shown in Figure 7.

claim: Higher novelty seeking scores were not correlated with stronger pain modulation induced by winning in the naltrexone condition.
source: In contrast, higher novelty seeking scores were not correlated with stronger pain modulation induced by winning in the naltrexone condition (r=0.153, p=0.381) and the naltrexone induced change in pain modulation showed no significant association with novelty seeking (r=0.239, p=0.499).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis in the naltrexone condition.

claim: Pain modulation after losing was not associated with novelty seeking in any drug condition.
source: Pain modulation after losing was not associated with novelty seeking in placebo (r=0.083, p=0.866), levodopa (r=–0.164, p=0.783), or naltrexone (r=0.405, p=0.133).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis for losing trials.

claim: The perception of relief is sensitive to endogenous modulation during motivated behavior.
source: The results show that (i) the perception of relief is sensitive to endogenous modulation during motivated behavior, (ii) this modulation scales with the informational content of the relief, being enhanced when relief is actively controllable, more unexpected, and especially in high trait novelty seeking individuals, (iii) this information-specific modulation is sensitive to manipulation of dopamine signaling, with no significant effects of the manipulation of opioidergic signaling on endogenous modulation; (iv) however, both dopaminergic and opioidergic signaling have an influence on relief-seeking, which may be at least in part dissociable from relief perception.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study findings.

claim: Relief modulation scales with the informational content of the relief, being enhanced when relief is actively controllable, more unexpected, and especially in high trait novelty seeking individuals.
source: The results show that (i) the perception of relief is sensitive to endogenous modulation during motivated behavior, (ii) this modulation scales with the informational content of the relief, being enhanced when relief is actively controllable, more unexpected, and especially in high trait novelty seeking individuals, (iii) this information-specific modulation is sensitive to manipulation of dopamine signaling, with no significant effects of the manipulation of opioidergic signaling on endogenous modulation; (iv) however, both dopaminergic and opioidergic signaling have an influence on relief-seeking, which may be at least in part dissociable from relief perception.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study findings.

claim: Information-specific modulation of relief is sensitive to manipulation of dopamine signaling.
source: The results show that (i) the perception of relief is sensitive to endogenous modulation during motivated behavior, (ii) this modulation scales with the informational content of the relief, being enhanced when relief is actively controllable, more unexpected, and especially in high trait novelty seeking individuals, (iii) this information-specific modulation is sensitive to manipulation of dopamine signaling, with no significant effects of the manipulation of opioidergic signaling on endogenous modulation; (iv) however, both dopaminergic and opioidergic signaling have an influence on relief-seeking, which may be at least in part dissociable from relief perception.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study findings.

claim: Both dopaminergic and opioidergic signaling have an influence on relief-seeking, which may be at least in part dissociable from relief perception.
source: The results show that (i) the perception of relief is sensitive to endogenous modulation during motivated behavior, (ii) this modulation scales with the informational content of the relief, being enhanced when relief is actively controllable, more unexpected, and especially in high trait novelty seeking individuals, (iii) this information-specific modulation is sensitive to manipulation of dopamine signaling, with no significant effects of the manipulation of opioidergic signaling on endogenous modulation; (iv) however, both dopaminergic and opioidergic signaling have an influence on relief-seeking, which may be at least in part dissociable from relief perception.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study findings.

claim: Dopaminergic signaling is involved in a fundamental component of the endogenous modulation of pain relief.
source: Overall, this shows that dopaminergic signaling is involved in a fundamental component of the endogenous modulation of pain relief.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study findings.

claim: Pain is increased in situations in which it has a more important role in shaping behavior, such as when it directs a change in behavior or when it is partly unpredictable.
source: That is, pain is increased in situations in which it has a more important role in shaping behavior – for instance when it directs a change in behavior (instrumentally controllable), when it is partly unpredictable (i.e. contains new information), and in otherwise dangerous contexts.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about pain modulation principles.

claim: Pain functions as a signal for behavioral control that is concerned with the prospective control of behavior.
source: This theory centralizes the functional role of pain as a signal for behavioral control that is concerned with the prospective control of behavior.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about pain function.

claim: The offset of pain is important as a control signal for guiding behavior in the context of an ongoing noxious event.
source: In principle, this can be extended as a potential account for the modulation of relief, because the offset of pain is also important as a control signal for guiding behavior, one which occurs in the context of an ongoing noxious event, such as an injury of some sort (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical extension supported by citation.

claim: Novelty seeking describes an explicit information-seeking tendency, in which new information is explored with the potential to lead to knowledge of better outcomes that can be exploited in the future.
source: This is because novelty seeking describes an explicit information-seeking tendency, in which new information is explored with the potential to lead to knowledge of better outcomes that can be exploited in the future (Wittmann et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: High trait novelty seekers might be more sensitive to information that occurs through relief outcomes.
source: This illustrates the common basis for intrinsic motivation for novelty and information-seeking for exploitable benefit, and hence we can predict that high trait novelty seekers might be more sensitive to information that occurs through relief outcomes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on theoretical reasoning about novelty seeking.

claim: The principles for controllability and unpredictability extended to increases in pain.
source: The principles for controllability and unpredictability also extended to increases in pain, consistent with the notion that increases in tonic pain act in a similar way to phasic pain operating from a pain-free baseline.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings for pain increases.

claim: Increases in tonic pain act in a similar way to phasic pain operating from a pain-free baseline.
source: The principles for controllability and unpredictability also extended to increases in pain, consistent with the notion that increases in tonic pain act in a similar way to phasic pain operating from a pain-free baseline.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings for pain increases.

claim: Levodopa significantly strengthened the association of endogenous modulation of perception with the extent to which nociceptive input was unpredictable or surprising.
source: Levodopa significantly strengthened the association of endogenous modulation of the perception with the extent to which nociceptive input was unpredictable or surprising, suggesting that dopamine is involved in a fine-grained perceptual modulation that may help to control immediate reactions to pain related cues as well as to optimize prospective behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the levodopa findings on prediction errors.

claim: Dopamine is involved in a fine-grained perceptual modulation that may help to control immediate reactions to pain related cues as well as to optimize prospective behavior.
source: Levodopa significantly strengthened the association of endogenous modulation of the perception with the extent to which nociceptive input was unpredictable or surprising, suggesting that dopamine is involved in a fine-grained perceptual modulation that may help to control immediate reactions to pain related cues as well as to optimize prospective behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the levodopa findings on prediction errors.

claim: Effects of dopamine on pain perception are not unidirectional but depend on the motivational and the informational value of nociceptive signals.
source: Moreover, our results support the view that effects of dopamine on pain perception are not unidirectional but depend on the motivational and the informational value of nociceptive signals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall dopamine findings.

claim: The personality trait of novelty seeking has been associated with enhanced dopaminergic activity due to lower midbrain (auto)receptor availability.
source: Note that the personality trait of novelty seeking has also been associated with enhanced dopaminergic activity due to lower midbrain (auto)receptor availability (Leyton et al., 2002; Savage et al., 2014; Zald et al., 2008), which further supports a general role for dopamine in information-sensitive behavior (Kakade and Dayan, 2002; Vellani et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dopamine has a general role in information-sensitive behavior.
source: Note that the personality trait of novelty seeking has also been associated with enhanced dopaminergic activity due to lower midbrain (auto)receptor availability (Leyton et al., 2002; Savage et al., 2014; Zald et al., 2008), which further supports a general role for dopamine in information-sensitive behavior (Kakade and Dayan, 2002; Vellani et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dopamine release in the Nucleus accumbens was related to the development of conditioned place preference that could be blocked by dopamine antagonists.
source: The role of dopamine in pain relief in the context of reinforcement is supported by findings of increased dopamine release induced by pain relief in the Nucleus accumbens of rats (Navratilova et al., 2012; Xie et al., 2014). Dopamine release was related to the development of conditioned place preference that could be blocked by dopamine antagonists (Navratilova et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work in rats.

claim: Dopamine release in the Nucleus accumbens and conditioned place preference in response to pain relief depend on opioidergic signaling.
source: Further, Navratilova et al., 2015b showed that dopamine release in the Nucleus accumbens and conditioned place preference in response to pain relief depend on opioidergic signaling: both were blocked by opioid antagonism in the anterior cingulate cortex, an area encoding pain aversiveness.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Dopamine release and conditioned place preference were blocked by opioid antagonism in the anterior cingulate cortex.
source: Further, Navratilova et al., 2015b showed that dopamine release in the Nucleus accumbens and conditioned place preference in response to pain relief depend on opioidergic signaling: both were blocked by opioid antagonism in the anterior cingulate cortex, an area encoding pain aversiveness.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: 50 mg of naltrexone induces more than 90% blockage of μ-opioid receptors in humans.
source: The doses and methods used here are comparable to those used in other contexts which have identified opioidergic effects. Using positron emission tomography Weerts et al., 2013 found a blockage of μ-opioid receptors of more than 90% by 50 mg of naltrexone (p.o.) in humans given repeatedly over 4 days.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: 50 mg naltrexone attenuates wanting and liking of social rewards.
source: Chelnokova et al., 2014 found attenuating effects of 50 mg naltrexone (p.o.) on wanting as well as liking of social rewards, implicating the involvement of endogenous opioids in the processing of rewarding stimuli.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: 50 mg naltrexone attenuates reward directed effort in a value-based decision-making task.
source: The same dose was also found to attenuate reward directed effort exerted in a value-based decision-making task (Eikemo et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: 50 mg of naltrexone reduces endogenous pain inhibition induced by conditioned pain modulation.
source: Moreover, 50 mg of naltrexone (p.o.) have been shown to reduce endogenous pain inhibition induced by conditioned pain modulation (King et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The opioidergic manipulation was effective in this study.
source: Thus, based on the literature we assume that the opioidergic manipulation was effective in this study, although we do not have a direct manipulation check of this pharmacological manipulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior literature, acknowledging lack of direct manipulation check.

claim: The effect of naltrexone on reward responses was found to be small.
source: Despite its effectiveness in blocking endogenous opioid receptors, the effect of naltrexone on reward responses was found to be small (Rabiner et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A lack of power may have limited the chances to find naltrexone effects in the present study.
source: Hence, a lack of power may have limited our chances to find such effects in the present study.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential limitation of the study.

claim: Perception of passively received pain relief was reduced by blocking of opioid receptors.
source: In humans, Sirucek et al., 2021 showed that perception of passively received pain relief was reduced by blocking of opioid receptors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Increased opioid activity in the anterior cingulate cortex is associated with selectively decreased pain aversiveness with unaltered sensory pain components.
source: Increased opioid activity in the anterior cingulate cortex has been shown to be associated with selectively decreased pain aversiveness with unaltered sensory pain components (Gomtsian et al., 2019; Maruyama et al., 2018; Navratilova et al., 2015b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The affective dimension of enhanced relief perception by rewarding pain relief may be reduced by opioid blockade with the sensory component possibly being unaffected.
source: Future studies need to address the question whether the affective dimension of enhanced relief perception by rewarding pain relief may be reduced by opioid blockade with the sensory component possibly being unaffected.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: VAS ratings indicate perception of phasic changes (outcomes).
source: Although we did not assess the affective component of the relief experience, we implemented two outcome measures that are assumed to capture independent aspects of the pain experience: VAS ratings indicate perception of phasic changes (outcomes), while the behavioral measure indicates perceptual within-trial sensitization or habituation in response to the tonic stimulation within each trial.
evidence: This is a methodological explanation of the outcome measures.

claim: The behavioral measure indicates perceptual within-trial sensitization or habituation in response to the tonic stimulation within each trial.
source: Although we did not assess the affective component of the relief experience, we implemented two outcome measures that are assumed to capture independent aspects of the pain experience: VAS ratings indicate perception of phasic changes (outcomes), while the behavioral measure indicates perceptual within-trial sensitization or habituation in response to the tonic stimulation within each trial.
evidence: This is a methodological explanation of the outcome measures.

claim: Becker et al., 2015 found a reduction of within-trial sensitization after pain relief outcomes by active controllability.
source: In a previous study using a similar experimental paradigm Becker et al., 2015 found a reduction of within-trial sensitization after pain relief outcomes by active controllability.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Smaller changes in stimulation intensity as outcomes in the current study potentially explain the differential results compared to Becker et al., 2015.
source: Compared to this study we implemented smaller changes in stimulation intensity as outcomes in the wheel of fortune (–3 °C vs –7 °C for pain relief), potentially explaining the differential results.
evidence: This is speculation about why results differ from prior work.

claim: The data argue against a simple transposition of experienced relief into decision value.
source: However, the data argue against a simple transposition of experienced relief (measured by VAS) into decision value, which for a stationary task such as this, should lead to more deterministic actions in the levodopa condition but no effect under naltrexone compared to placebo.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the dissociation between relief perception and choice behavior.

claim: Multiple decision systems ('model-based' and 'model-free') might be involved in even simple instrumental tasks.
source: The association of explicit contingency awareness and choice in our task illustrates the fact that multiple decision systems ('model-based' and 'model-free') might be involved in even simple instrumental tasks, and hence that more sophisticated task manipulations are needed to decompose these different components (Langdon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation to prior work on decision systems.

claim: There is at least a simple dissociation between the drug effects on experienced relief and decision-making.
source: However, our key finding is that there is at least a simple dissociation between the drug effects on experienced relief and decision-making.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding.

claim: Dopamine has been related to instrumental learning due to its prominent role in mediating reward and aversive prediction errors.
source: Dopamine has been related to instrumental learning due to its prominent role in mediating reward and aversive prediction errors (Glimcher, 2011; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Schultz, 2007; Schultz, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Effects of dopaminergic modulation on value-based decision making and brain activity related to reward prediction errors in the Nucleus accumbens have been reported.
source: Correspondingly, effects of dopaminergic modulation on value-based decision making and brain activity related to reward prediction errors in the Nucleus accumbens have been reported (Pessiglione et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Impaired learning functions under dopaminergic medication are known from research in Parkinson's disease.
source: On the other hand, impaired learning functions under dopaminergic medication are known from research in Parkinson's disease (Breitenstein et al., 2006; Pizzagalli et al., 2008; Santesso et al., 2009; Vo et al., 2016) and have been attributed to dopamine overstimulation (Cools et al., 2001; Vaillancourt et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dopamine overstimulation does not impair learning of associations or reward expectations, but only the transfer to overt actions.
source: Others argued that dopamine overstimulation does not impair learning of associations or reward expectations, but only the transfer to overt actions (choice behavior; Beeler, 2012; Beeler et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Levodopa reduced model-free control of choice behavior while neural reward prediction error signals and model-based learning remained unaffected.
source: Accordingly, Kroemer et al., 2019 found reduced model-free control of choice behavior under levodopa (i.e. a decrease in direct reinforcement of actions by rewards) while both, neural reward prediction error signals and also model-based learning remained unaffected.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Increased dopamine availability might have led to increased explorative behavior in the present task.
source: Given the involvement of multiple decision systems in our task increased dopamine availability might have led to increased explorative behavior. When exploration is favored over exploitation choice behavior is less driven by values learned from the prior reward history.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the levodopa effects on choice.

claim: Dopamine has been implicated in motivational aspects (incentive salience) of reward processing.
source: At the same time, dopamine has also been implicated in motivational aspects (incentive salience) of reward processing (Berridge et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2011; Tindell et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dopamine may have increased motivational drive and related facilitation of pain modulation while at the same time increased dopamine availability may have reduced the expression of prior reward learning.
source: Hence, dopamine may have increased motivational drive and related facilitation of pain modulation in the present task, while at the same time increased dopamine availability may have reduced the expression of prior reward learning (Beeler, 2012).
evidence: This is speculation about the dual role of dopamine in the present task, supported by citation.

claim: Opioids have been related to both incentive salience and the hedonic value of rewards.
source: Opioids have been related to both, incentive salience and the hedonic value of rewards (Berridge et al., 2009; Meier et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Opioid agonism increases while opioid antagonism decreases 'wanting' and 'liking' of attractive faces.
source: In humans, bidirectional manipulations have shown that opioid agonism increases while opioid antagonism decreases "wanting" (i.e. incentive salience) as well as "liking" of attractive faces (Chelnokova et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Opioid manipulations affect motivation and choice behavior for monetary rewards.
source: The same mechanism was also shown for the effort to work for and the response bias for higher monetary rewards indicating that opioid manipulations affect motivation but also choice behavior (Eikemo et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Inhibition of opioidergic activity by blocking endogenous opioid receptors could impair reward processing, explaining why participants did not develop a preference for the better choice option under naltrexone.
source: These findings suggest that inhibition of opioidergic activity by blocking endogenous opioid receptors could impair reward processing (independent of effects of endogenous opioids on pain modulation), and hence, explain why participants did not develop a preference for the choice option that was associated with a higher chance to win pain relief under naltrexone in the present task.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the naltrexone effects on choice.

claim: The mechanisms underlying learning from pain and pain relief and their recursive influence on pain perception may contribute to the development and maintenance of chronic pain.
source: Because the mechanisms underlying learning from pain and pain relief and their recursive influence on pain perception may contribute to the development and maintenance of chronic pain, it is crucial to better understand the roles of dopamine and endogenous opioids in these mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical relevance of the research.

claim: Reward learning plays a role in the transition of acute to chronic pain.
source: Reward learning has recently been shown to play a role in the transition of acute to chronic pain with a specific pattern of Nucleus accumbens activity in response to a cue predicting pain relief being predictive for chronification (Löffler et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Pain relief processing is a potential leverage point for prevention strategies.
source: This makes pain relief processing a potential leverage point for prevention strategies.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited work on reward learning and chronic pain.

claim: Levodopa or dopamine agonists could have a potential adjuvant role in management programs when used in the context of rehabilitation strategies that aim to harness endogenous control mechanisms.
source: Although levodopa or dopamine agonists are not generally used as analgesics in the clinical management of chronic pain, it may be that they could have a potential adjuvant role in management programs, for example when used in the context of rehabilitation strategies that aim to harness endogenous control mechanisms.
evidence: This is speculation about potential clinical applications.

claim: Parkinson's disease has a well-recognized association with chronic pain, beyond that which can be explained by motor effects.
source: It is also worth noting that Parkinson's disease has a well-recognized association with chronic pain, beyond that which can be explained by motor effects, and in keeping with a potential core role for dopamine in the pathogenesis of chronic pain in some contexts (Beiske et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Dopamine has a core role in pain relief information processing, by which it modulates the way in which information tunes the modulation of pain to meet motivational demands.
source: In summary, our study shows that dopamine has a core role in pain relief information processing, by which it modulates the way in which information tunes the modulation of pain to meet motivational demands.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.
